evidence: pulse innovates on three key design elements (Fig. 3).
The iterator code provided by the data structure developer is translated into pulse's instruction set architecture
pulse supports scalable distributed pointer traversals by leveraging programmable network switches

summary: pulse is a distributed pointer-traversal framework for rack-scale disaggregated memory. This figure gives an end-to-end overview of its three key design elements. On the left, application code sits atop a data-structure library that exposes pulse's iterator interface, letting developers port linked-data-structure traversals with minimal effort; a dispatch engine then translates that iterator code into pulse's instruction set architecture (ISA), running on CPU nodes. The translated code, bounded by a computation limit, crosses a network built from programmable switches, which route requests to the appropriate memory node. Each memory node embeds a PULSE Accelerator that executes the ISA instructions using disaggregated logic and memory pipelines, and, when a traversal's target address is not local, hands the request back to the switch for distributed continuation to the correct memory node. Section-number callouts (§3, §4.1, §4.2, §5) tie each stage to where it is detailed in the text.
